messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 77
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Delivery Driver
- Trauma Type: Assault
- Pcl5: 48

He still drives his delivery route, but the familiar streets have become a maze of invisible threats. At seventy-seven, Raymond has spent forty years behind the wheel of his small delivery truck, navigating the same suburban neighborhoods, handing packages to the same friendly faces. He knows every shortcut, every house with a dog, every cul-de-sac where he can turn around without backing up. That knowledge used to make him feel competent, even proud. Now it makes him feel like a target.

The assault happened eight months ago, on a Tuesday afternoon in late October. He was making his usual stop at a strip mall, delivering a heavy box to a pharmacy in the back corner. He remembers the way the afternoon sun slanted through the glass storefront, how it cast long shadows on the linoleum floor. He remembers the man—young, maybe twenty-five, with a faded hoodie and restless eyes—who stepped out from behind a display of greeting cards and asked for the time. Raymond remembers reaching for his wristwatch, and then the explosion of pain as the man’s fist connected with the side of his head, the world turning sideways, the floor rushing up to meet him. He never saw the punch coming. He never saw the man’s face again, only the blur of sneakers running toward the exit. The security footage was useless—the man’s hood had been pulled low.

Raymond spent two nights in the hospital with a mild concussion and three broken ribs from where he’d landed on the edge of a display shelf. The doctors said he was lucky. His wife, Edith, said the same thing, her hand trembling as she held his in the emergency room. But Raymond does not feel lucky. He feels hollowed out, as though the punch knocked something loose inside him that cannot be put back.

Now, every time he approaches a delivery, his heart begins to pound before he even opens the truck door. He parks as close as possible to the entrance, scanning the area for anyone who might be hiding behind a pillar or a parked car. He hates that he does this. He knows it’s irrational—the same strip mall, the same afternoon light, the same ordinary customers. But his body does not listen to reason. His hands shake when he hands over a package. His voice comes out thinner than it used to. Customers have started to ask if he’s feeling okay.

At night, he lies awake in the bedroom he has shared with Edith for fifty-two years. The memory of the assault plays on a loop behind his closed eyes: the young man’s shadow stretching toward him, the fist, the terrible crack in his skull, the taste of blood and dust. He jerks awake gasping, convinced he hears footsteps in the hallway. Edith sleeps beside him, her breathing even and slow. He does not wake her. He gets up and walks through the house, checking the locks on every door, the windows, the basement hatch. He knows the doors are locked. He checks them anyway.

His driving has changed. He takes longer routes now, avoiding streets where he might have to stop and get out, avoiding alleyways, avoiding any place where a stranger could approach without warning. His boss has noticed the delays and told him to “shake it off.” Raymond nodded, said nothing. He cannot explain that the world feels full of hidden fists, that every person who steps out from behind a corner is a potential threat, that he no longer trusts the ordinary safety of a Tuesday afternoon.

Edith asks him why he seems so jumpy, why he flinches when she touches his shoulder from behind. He tells her it’s nothing, just his age, just the stress of the job. He cannot bring himself to say that he replays the assault in his mind every single day, that he feels shame for not fighting back, that he dreads the moment he has to step out of his truck and into a world that can hurt him without warning.

The PCL-5 he filled out in the clinic waiting room scored a 48. He doesn’t know what that number means. He only knows that he cannot remember what it felt like to drive without checking the rearview mirror three times, to walk into a store without scanning every corner, to sleep through the night without fighting off the ghost of a young man in a hoodie.
